source_refs.note: Book p. 291-292: 11.4 Derivative Of A Vector-Valued Function: definition by limit, componentwise derivative, printed Examples 4-5 (shown as Examples 6-7)

blocks.text:
A vector-valued function of a single variable is a function that maps a scalar (usually time \(t\)) to a vector in \(\mathbb{R}^n\). For a function in three-dimensional space, it is typically written as:
\[\mathbf{r}(t) = \langle f_1(t), f_2(t), f_3(t)\rangle\]
\[= f_1(t)\,\hat{i} + f_2(t)\,\hat{j} + f_3(t)\,\hat{k}\]

Where \(\hat{i}, \hat{j}, \hat{k}\) are the unit vectors associated with the rectangular coordinates and \(f_1(t), f_2(t)\), and \(f_3(t)\) are scalar functions of \(t\), are the components of the vector-valued function \(\mathbf{r}(t)\).
book_errors: are scalar functions of \(t\), are the components

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The sentence has two verbs for one subject. It should read: "... and \(f_1(t), f_2(t)\) and \(f_3(t)\), which are scalar functions of \(t\), are the components of the vector-valued function \(\mathbf{r}(t)\)."

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: This is the same idea as 11.1.2: one input \(t\), and the output is a vector whose three components \(f_1, f_2, f_3\) are ordinary (scalar) functions of \(t\). For example, in \(\mathbf{r}(t) = t^2\,\hat{i} + \sin t\,\hat{j} + e^t\,\hat{k}\) the components are \(f_1 = t^2\), \(f_2 = \sin t\), \(f_3 = e^t\). A 2D function simply has no \(\hat{k}\)-term (\(f_3 = 0\)).
The derivative of a vector-valued function \(\mathbf{r}(t)\) with respect to \(t\) is defined as:

blocks.text_alt: d r by d t equals r prime of t equals the limit as delta t tends to 0 of r of t plus delta t minus r of t, all over delta t

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
This is the same difference quotient as for an ordinary function \(f(x)\) (Unit 2), only now the top is a vector.
\(\mathbf{r}(t + \Delta t) - \mathbf{r}(t)\) is the small change in position (the chord vector from one point of the curve to a nearby point). Dividing by \(\Delta t\) gives the average rate of change, and the limit \(\Delta t \to 0\) gives the instantaneous rate of change: a vector along the tangent to the curve. In 11.5 this is the velocity.
If the limit exists, then \(\mathbf{r}'(t)\) is computed by differentiating each component:

blocks.text_alt: r prime of t equals the ordered triple f 1 prime of t, f 2 prime of t, f 3 prime of t
equals f 1 prime of t times i hat plus f 2 prime of t times j hat plus f 3 prime of t times k hat

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why component by component? Write the difference quotient in components:
\[\dfrac{\mathbf{r}(t + \Delta t) - \mathbf{r}(t)}{\Delta t}\]
\[= \dfrac{f_1(t + \Delta t) - f_1(t)}{\Delta t}\,\hat{i} + \dots\]
The unit vectors \(\hat{i}, \hat{j}, \hat{k}\) are constant, so they stay outside, and the limit of each component is that component's ordinary derivative \(f_1'(t), f_2'(t), f_3'(t)\). So all the rules of Unit 2 (power, product, quotient, chain) work, one component at a time.
\(\mathbf{r}'(t)\) exists only where every component has a derivative.

blocks.title: Numbering note (ours)
blocks.text: The book prints the two examples of this section as Example 4 and Example 5. Its example numbering starts again at 1 in 11.2 (after Examples 1 and 2 of 11.1.3), so two different examples of this unit already carry each of the numbers 1 and 2. To give every example of Unit 11 its own number, we count them in one sequence: the book's Example 4 and Example 5 appear here as Example 6 and Example 7.

blocks.title: Example 6
blocks.problem: Find the first derivative of \(\mathbf{r}(t) = t^2\,\hat{i} + \sin t\,\hat{j} + e^t\,\hat{k}\) with respect to \(t\).
steps:
Given: \(\mathbf{r}(t) = t^2\,\hat{i} + \sin t\,\hat{j} + e^t\,\hat{k}\).
To find: \(\mathbf{r}'(t)\).
Method: by the definition above, differentiate each component separately and keep it with its own unit vector.

Differentiate each component separately
\[\dfrac{d}{dt}(t^2) = 2t\]
\[\dfrac{d}{dt}(\sin t) = \cos t\]
\[\dfrac{d}{dt}(e^t) = e^t\]
Why: power rule; the standard derivatives of \(\sin t\) and \(e^t\).

Put them back with the unit vectors
\[\mathbf{r}'(t) = 2t\,\hat{i} + \cos t\,\hat{j} + e^t\,\hat{k}\]
Why: \(\mathbf{r}'(t) = f_1'(t)\,\hat{i} + f_2'(t)\,\hat{j} + f_3'(t)\,\hat{k}\).

Check at \(t = 0\)
\[\mathbf{r}'(0) = 0\,\hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k}\]
With \(\Delta t = 0.001\): \(\frac{\mathbf{r}(0.001) - \mathbf{r}(0)}{0.001} \approx 0.001\,\hat{i} + 1.000\,\hat{j} + 1.0005\,\hat{k}\), very close \(\checkmark\).

blocks.title: Example 7
blocks.problem: Find the first derivative of \(\mathbf{r}(t) = \sec t\,\hat{i} + \tan t\,\hat{j} - \cos t\,\hat{k}\) at \(t = \frac{\pi}{4}\).
steps:
Given: \(\mathbf{r}(t) = \sec t\,\hat{i} + \tan t\,\hat{j} - \cos t\,\hat{k}\), \(t = \frac{\pi}{4}\).
To find: \(\mathbf{r}'\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right)\).
Method: differentiate each component separately, then find its value at \(t = \frac{\pi}{4}\), using \(\sin\frac{\pi}{4} = \cos\frac{\pi}{4} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\).

\(\hat{i}\)-component
\[\dfrac{d}{dt}(\sec t) = \sec t \cdot \tan t\]
\[\left.\dfrac{d(\sec t)}{dt}\right|_{t = \pi/4} = \sec\tfrac{\pi}{4}\tan\tfrac{\pi}{4}\]
\[= \sqrt{2} \cdot 1 = \sqrt{2}\]
Why: standard derivative of \(\sec t\); \(\sec\frac{\pi}{4} = \frac{1}{\cos(\pi/4)} = \sqrt{2}\), \(\tan\frac{\pi}{4} = 1\).

\(\hat{j}\)-component
\[\dfrac{d}{dt}(\tan t) = \sec^2 t\]
\[\left.\dfrac{d(\tan t)}{dt}\right|_{t = \pi/4} = \sec^2\tfrac{\pi}{4}\]
\[= (\sqrt{2})^2 = 2\]
Why: standard derivative of \(\tan t\).

\(\hat{k}\)-component
\[\dfrac{d}{dt}(-\cos t) = \sin t\]
\[\left.\dfrac{d(-\cos t)}{dt}\right|_{t = \pi/4} = \sin\tfrac{\pi}{4} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\]
Why: \(\frac{d}{dt}\cos t = -\sin t\), and the minus sign in front makes it \(+\sin t\).

Put them together
\[\mathbf{r}'\left(\tfrac{\pi}{4}\right) = \sqrt{2}\,\hat{i} + 2\,\hat{j} + \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\,\hat{k}\]
Why: each value goes with its own unit vector.

Check
\(\mathbf{r}'(t) = \sec t\tan t\,\hat{i} + \sec^2 t\,\hat{j} + \sin t\,\hat{k}\); at \(t = \frac{\pi}{4}\) a computer algebra system gives \(\sqrt{2}\,\hat{i} + 2\,\hat{j} + \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\,\hat{k}\), the same since \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\) \(\checkmark\).

blocks.title: Exam tip
blocks.text: When the derivative is asked "at" a value of \(t\): first differentiate each component in general, then substitute. Substituting first turns each component into a constant, whose derivative is 0.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. \(\mathbf{r}(t) = f_1(t)\,\hat{i} + f_2(t)\,\hat{j} + f_3(t)\,\hat{k}\): the components are scalar functions of \(t\).
2. Definition: \(\mathbf{r}'(t) = \lim_{\Delta t \to 0}\frac{\mathbf{r}(t + \Delta t) - \mathbf{r}(t)}{\Delta t}\).
3. In practice: \(\mathbf{r}'(t) = f_1'(t)\,\hat{i} + f_2'(t)\,\hat{j} + f_3'(t)\,\hat{k}\); all the usual rules apply to each component.
4. \(\hat{i}, \hat{j}, \hat{k}\) are constants: they are not differentiated.
5. \(\mathbf{r}'(t)\) is a vector tangent to the curve (the velocity in 11.5).

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Differentiating the unit vectors, or dropping them: each derivative must stay with its own \(\hat{i}\), \(\hat{j}\) or \(\hat{k}\).
2. Substituting the value of \(t\) before differentiating.
3. Sign slips: \(\frac{d}{dt}(-\cos t) = +\sin t\), not \(-\sin t\).
4. Forgetting that a missing term (no \(\hat{j}\), say) is a zero component with zero derivative.
